texts.0: SP, due to a late and coarse pitch response to the simulated engine failure, did not hold the ELP airspeed schedule between high key and low key. Airspeed diverged to 22 knots above and later to 14 knots below the target, exceeding the +15 / -10 knots limit in both directions. The IP intervened on the controls to restore the glide speed before base key.
texts.1: SP, due to a pitch input that chased the ELP airspeed instead of setting an attitude, did not stabilize the glide speed after high key. Airspeed reached 15 knots fast on the descent and 10 knots slow in the turn to final, sitting on the +15 / -10 knots limit. The correction was applied only after repeated verbal prompting by the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a trim setting left unchanged after the simulated failure, did not maintain the ELP airspeed within the tighter tolerance. Airspeed drifted to 13 knots fast approaching low key and 8 knots slow on final, between the +10 / -5 and +15 / -10 knots bands. SP recognized both excursions and recovered the schedule without any input from the IP.
texts.3: SP set the glide attitude promptly after the simulated failure and flew the ELP airspeed schedule accurately from high key to touchdown. Deviations remained inside +10 / -5 knots throughout the pattern, including the configuration changes and the turn to final. Corrections were small, timely and made with trim rather than with pressure on the stick.
texts.4: SP captured the ELP glide speed within seconds of the simulated failure and held it essentially on target for the whole pattern. Airspeed excursions did not exceed a few knots even during gear and flap extension and through the final turn. Speed control at the round out left ample margin above the stall.
texts.marginal: SP kept the ELP airspeed inside the required tolerance, but the trace shows a consistent bias to the fast side that grew through the descending turns. Corrections were correct in direction yet late enough that the deviation reached the outer part of the acceptable band before it was arrested. SP is expected to set and trim the glide speed earlier so that the schedule is held near the target rather than near the limit.

texts.0: SP, due to a pattern flown without reference to the computed key point altitudes, did not arrive at high key and low key at the planned heights. The aircraft was 420 feet high at high key and 260 feet low at low key, outside the +300 / -200 feet limit. The IP took control to reposition the pattern and preserve a safe glide to the runway.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed assessment of the wind effect on the descending pattern, did not correct the energy state between key points. Altitude was 300 feet high at low key and 200 feet low at base key, exactly at the +300 / -200 feet limit. SP began the correction only after the IP called the deviation twice.
texts.2: SP, due to a bank angle held shallower than required in the turn from high key, did not track the planned altitude profile. The aircraft passed low key 230 feet high and base key 170 feet low, between the plus or minus 150 feet and the +300 / -200 feet bands. SP identified the error at low key and adjusted the ground track in time to regain the profile on final.
texts.3: SP flew the ELP so that high key, low key and base key were all reached within plus or minus 150 feet of the planned altitudes. Bank angle and ground track were adjusted continuously to protect the energy state as the pattern developed. The resulting glide gave a comfortable margin to the intended touchdown point.
texts.4: SP arrived at every key point within a few tens of feet of the planned altitude, with no visible correction required between them. The pattern was adjusted continuously and almost imperceptibly for the observed wind. Energy management at base key left the runway comfortably makeable with the flaps still available.
texts.marginal: SP met the key point altitudes within standards, but each point was reached on the high side with the excess energy carried forward rather than dissipated. The pattern remained flyable only because the final turn was tightened. SP is expected to assess the altitude at high key against the plan and to correct the ground track earlier so that low key and base key are reached closer to the planned figures.

error_modes.label: ELP planning to touch down within the first third of the runway

texts.0: SP, due to an aim point selected without reference to the available glide, did not plan the ELP to touch down within the first third of the runway. The projected touchdown was well beyond the first third and the approach could not be salvaged with the remaining energy. The IP took the aircraft and initiated a go around.
texts.1: SP, due to a late decision on where to place the aim point, did not protect the intended touchdown zone. The aircraft was tracking to touch down at the very end of the first third with no margin remaining, and SP adjusted the profile only after the IP prompted a correction on final.
texts.2: SP, due to an aim point set slightly deep for the observed headwind, did not initially plan the touchdown as required. The projected point moved past the first quarter of the runway, but SP recognized the trend at base key and used the ground track and flap timing to bring the touchdown back inside the first third without any input from the IP.
texts.3: SP planned the ELP with a correctly chosen aim point and touched down within the first third of the runway. The energy state at base key was assessed against the actual wind and the pattern was adjusted accordingly. The touchdown point matched the one briefed for the exercise.
texts.4: SP planned the ELP so precisely that the aircraft arrived over the threshold with the intended energy and touched down close to the briefed point inside the first third. The plan was visibly revised in flight as the wind effect became apparent, with no loss of accuracy. The result would have left the maximum usable runway available in a real forced landing.
texts.marginal: SP touched down within the first third of the runway, but consistently in its last portion, leaving little margin for a misjudged flare or a stronger headwind. The plan was sound in principle yet the aim point was set deeper than the exercise intends. SP is expected to select the aim point earlier and to bias the plan short so that the touchdown falls comfortably inside the first third.

texts.0: SP, due to inadequate workload management during the approach phase, did not configure the aircraft timely and correctly in the ELP. Gear and flaps were selected out of sequence and well after the planned points, leaving the aircraft unconfigured inside base key and the glide unable to reach the touchdown zone. The IP intervened to complete the configuration and terminate the pattern.
texts.1: SP, due to inadequate workload management during the approach phase, did not complete the ELP configuration at the planned points. Gear selection was delayed until after low key and landing flaps were set only on short final, so the drag change arrived too late to be flown out smoothly. The configuration was completed only after the IP called for it.
texts.2: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated all cockpit workload inside the turn, did not configure the aircraft at the briefed points. Gear and flap selections were made noticeably late relative to low key, but SP recognized the compression, resequenced the remaining actions and had the aircraft fully configured on final with the airspeed schedule intact.
texts.3: SP configured the aircraft timely and correctly throughout the ELP, with gear and flap selections made at the briefed points and in the correct order. Each configuration change was flown out with pitch and trim so that the airspeed schedule was preserved. Cockpit workload remained distributed across the pattern.
texts.4: SP anticipated every configuration change in the ELP and made each selection at the correct point with the aircraft in trim and the speed on schedule. Drag changes produced no detectable excursion in airspeed or descent rate. Workload was managed so that the pattern was flown with capacity remaining for the simulated restart actions.
texts.marginal: SP configured the aircraft correctly and within the accepted window, but each selection was made at the late edge of that window and the actions bunched together approaching low key. The airspeed schedule held only because the corrections that followed were prompt. SP is expected to anticipate the gear and flap points and to spread the configuration actions across the pattern rather than compressing them into the turn.

texts.0: SP, due to a lack of knowledge of the engine restart procedure required for this exercise, did not demonstrate cognizance of it or execute it in simulation. The steps were attempted in the wrong order and critical items were omitted, and the attempt consumed attention that was needed to fly the pattern. The IP stopped the simulated procedure and took the aircraft to restore the ELP profile.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete recall of the engine restart procedure, did not execute it in simulation without assistance. Several items were called out of sequence and the attempt was completed only after the IP prompted each remaining step, delaying the actions past low key.
texts.2: SP, due to an interrupted recall of the restart sequence under the workload of the pattern, did not initially execute the simulated procedure in the correct order. SP paused, identified the omitted item and completed the procedure correctly before base key without any prompting from the IP, and the flight path was not affected.
texts.3: SP demonstrated clear cognizance of the engine restart procedure and executed it in simulation at the appropriate point in the pattern. The items were called and actioned in the correct order while the ELP profile continued to be flown accurately. The simulation did not degrade the aircraft control or the pattern geometry.
texts.4: SP executed the simulated engine restart with immediate and complete recall of the procedure, integrating it into the pattern without any interruption of the scan. The sequence was verbalized clearly for the IP and completed with time in hand before low key. The airmanship shown in dividing attention between the procedure and the glide was of a high standard.
texts.marginal: SP knew the engine restart procedure and executed it in simulation acceptably, but the recall was hesitant and each item required a visible pause before it was actioned. Attention was drawn inside the cockpit for longer than the pattern comfortably allows. SP is expected to bring the procedure to the point of immediate recall so that the simulation costs no attention from the glide.

error_modes.label: Stall margin and low speed handling

texts.0: SP, due to an attempt to stretch the glide to the intended touchdown point, did not prevent the appearance of stall characteristics in the final turn. Airspeed decayed well below the ELP schedule with buffet and stall warning present, and the recovery required advancing the throttle. The IP intervened on the controls to unload the aircraft and terminate the pattern.
texts.1: SP, due to a nose up pitch input held in the turn to final to protect the aim point, did not maintain the required stall margin. Airspeed fell to the low limit of the schedule with the stall warning triggering briefly, and SP relaxed the back pressure only after the IP called the speed.
texts.2: SP, due to increased back pressure applied during the final flap extension, did not preserve the intended speed margin. Airspeed decayed toward the low end of the acceptable band with no stall indications, and SP recognized the decay, lowered the nose and restored the schedule without any input from the IP or use of the throttle.
texts.3: SP flew the ELP with the stall margin protected throughout, including the final turn and the round out. No stall characteristics appeared at any point and the throttle was not required to recover the aircraft state. Bank angle and back pressure were traded correctly to preserve the speed.
texts.4: SP maintained a comfortable and consistent margin above the stall at every stage of the ELP, with the final turn flown at a bank and speed combination that left the aircraft well clear of the buffet. Control inputs were smooth and the flare was flown with the energy planned rather than borrowed. There was never any tendency toward a condition requiring throttle to recover.
texts.marginal: SP kept the aircraft clear of stall characteristics, but the final turn was flown at the low edge of the speed schedule with the margin thinner than the exercise intends. No warning appeared, yet the combination of bank and speed left little tolerance for a gust. SP is expected to protect the speed by adjusting the aim point rather than the pitch attitude when the glide appears short.

error_modes.label: ELP termination as touch and go or go around

texts.0: SP, due to continuation bias in maintaining the approach after the conditions had deteriorated below the briefed minima, did not terminate the ELP as a touch and go or a go around as required. SP continued toward a full stop from an approach that no longer met the parameters for the exercise. The IP took control and executed the go around.
texts.1: SP, due to continuation of the plan after the information that invalidated it had already been received, did not initiate the go around at the point where the ELP could no longer produce an acceptable touchdown. The termination was flown correctly but only after a direct instruction from the IP, by which time the aircraft was inside the last acceptable point for the decision.
texts.2: SP, due to a late reassessment of the energy state on short final, did not decide on the termination as early as the exercise requires. SP recognized without prompting that the touchdown zone could not be met, called and flew a clean go around, and the aircraft never approached an unsafe state.
texts.3: SP terminated the ELP correctly as a touch and go, with the decision made in good time and the transition flown to the published technique. Configuration and power were applied in the correct sequence and the runway was used as planned. The termination was stated clearly to the IP before it was flown.
texts.4: SP assessed the approach early, stated the intended termination and flew a precise touch and go with the aircraft on speed and on the centerline. The decision point was respected without any prompting and the transition was seamless. The judgment shown in selecting between touch and go and go around was exactly as briefed.
texts.marginal: SP terminated the ELP correctly, but the decision was made close to the last usable point and the announcement to the IP came after the action had begun. The execution itself was sound. SP is expected to assess the approach earlier and to state the intended termination before reaching short final.

error_modes.label: Pattern geometry and wind correction between key points

texts.0: SP, due to a ground track flown without any allowance for the reported wind, did not position the ELP pattern so that the runway remained makeable. The aircraft was displaced far downwind of the intended track and arrived at base key with the runway unreachable on the available glide. The IP took control to recover the pattern.
texts.1: SP, due to a wind correction applied only after the drift had become obvious, did not hold the planned ground track between high key and low key. The displacement was large enough that the final turn had to be flown at an abnormally steep bank, and the correction was made only after the IP pointed out the drift.
texts.2: SP, due to a bank angle held constant instead of varied for the drift, did not track the planned pattern on the downwind side. The aircraft was displaced noticeably wide at low key, but SP identified the drift, tightened the turn progressively and rolled out on final aligned with the runway without any assistance.
texts.3: SP flew the ELP pattern with the ground track correctly adjusted for the wind, varying the bank angle to keep the aircraft in a position from which the runway remained makeable. Roll out on final was aligned with the centerline and required only small corrections. The geometry supported the planned touchdown point.
texts.4: SP corrected for the wind continuously and precisely from high key onward, keeping the pattern geometry within a very tight band of the plan. The final turn required no unusual bank and the aircraft rolled out on centerline at the planned altitude and speed. The pattern would have been flyable to the same accuracy in a real forced landing.
texts.marginal: SP kept the pattern within a workable geometry, but each turn was rolled out slightly wide and the accumulated displacement had to be taken out in the final turn. The wind correction was reactive rather than planned. SP is expected to assess the drift at high key and to build the correction into the pattern rather than removing it on final.

error_modes.label: Coordination with IP and ATC during the simulated emergency

texts.0: SP, due to a CRM breakdown in which the required behavior of explicit role assignment was not performed, did not coordinate the simulated emergency with the IP and ATC. The ELP was begun without confirming the IP command and the required calls were never made, so the pattern was flown without a shared plan. The IP took control and terminated the exercise.
texts.1: SP, due to inadequate crew coordination between front and rear cockpit, did not keep the IP informed of the intended profile or complete the required transmissions in time. The calls were made only after the IP directed each one, and the position report reached ATC after the aircraft was already established in the pattern.
texts.2: SP, due to an unshared assessment of the aircraft state between front and rear cockpit, did not initially communicate the change of plan when the pattern was adjusted. SP recognized the omission, briefed the IP on the revised aim point and completed the required calls before base key without any prompting.
texts.3: SP coordinated the simulated emergency correctly, acknowledging the IP command, verbalizing the intended pattern and completing the required calls at the appropriate points. The IP was kept informed of the energy state and of the planned termination. Radio work did not interfere with flying the ELP.
texts.4: SP handled the coordination with the IP and ATC to a standard well above the level of training, stating the plan, the key points and the intended termination clearly and in good time. Every transmission was concise and correctly timed, and the IP had a complete picture of the SP intentions throughout. Communication was fitted around the flying rather than competing with it.
texts.marginal: SP coordinated adequately with the IP and ATC, but the calls came late in each phase and the intended termination was communicated only on short final. Nothing was omitted. SP is expected to state the plan and the intended termination earlier so that the IP is not left inferring the SP intentions from the flight path.

error_modes.label: Initial actions after the simulated failure: turn, climb, clean, check and BIP

texts.0: SP, due to the turn toward the nearest suitable field being delayed while the simulated malfunction was still being analyzed, did not fly the initial actions in the turn, climb, clean, check and BIP sequence. The zoom was started late and flattened well short of the 20 degree climb angle, so the aircraft reached the pattern more than 400 feet below the key point altitude and more than 20 knots off the glide speed, outside the +300 / -200 feet and the +15 / -10 knots limits. The IP took the controls to reposition the aircraft on the ELP profile.
texts.1: SP, due to the turn to the field being started only after the checks were recalled, did not order the initial actions as turn, climb, clean, check and BIP. The late zoom and the shallow climb angle left the aircraft 200 feet low at the first key point and 15 knots fast, sitting on the +300 / -200 feet and +15 / -10 knots limits. SP repositioned the aircraft onto the profile only after repeated verbal prompting from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to the zoom being flown with less than the 2 G pull required to reach the 20 degree climb angle, did not convert the excess airspeed above 150 KIAS into the planned altitude. The aircraft entered the pattern about 250 feet low and 12 knots off the glide speed, between the tighter +150 feet and +10 / -5 knots band and the outer limits. SP recognized the energy shortfall against the key point picture and corrected the profile without any input from the IP.
texts.3: SP turned immediately toward the nearest suitable field, zoomed the excess airspeed above 150 KIAS into altitude and then cleaned, checked and set the boost pump and ignition switches as required. The aircraft was established on the ELP profile with the key point altitude held within 150 feet and the glide speed within +10 / -5 knots. The sequence was flown without prompting and the plan for the pattern entry was stated before high key.
texts.4: SP reacted to the simulated failure with an immediate turn toward the field and a zoom that was recovered right as the airspeed approached 20 KIAS above the glide speed. Clean up, checks and the BIP items followed in order and were completed well before the pattern entry, with the key point altitude off by only a few tens of feet and the glide speed steady within a few knots. The energy traded in the zoom matched the profile requirement almost exactly.
texts.marginal: SP flew the turn, climb, clean, check and BIP items in the correct order and stayed inside the required tolerances, but each step was started a few seconds after the previous one had already been prompted by the situation rather than by the plan. The accumulated delay pushed the entry altitude toward the low side of the acceptable band before the profile was regained. SP is expected to run the initial actions as one continuous flow so that the energy is protected at the start rather than recovered later.

error_modes.label: Clean up of excess drag and its effect on glide range

texts.0: SP, due to the clean up step being omitted after the simulated failure, left the landing gear and speed brake extended during the climb and the glide toward the field. With the gear down the glide ratio fell from 2:1 to about 1.5:1, and the aircraft arrived at the pattern more than 350 feet low with the airspeed more than 15 knots off the glide schedule, beyond the +300 / -200 feet and the +15 / -10 knots limits. The IP intervened to clean the aircraft and to re-plan the entry point.
texts.1: SP, due to the speed brake being left out while the checks were being read, did not clean the aircraft as soon as possible after the simulated failure. The residual drag cost enough glide range to put the aircraft 200 feet low at the key point with the speed 10 knots slow, on the -200 feet and -10 knots limits. SP retracted the drag devices only after the IP pointed out the configuration twice.
texts.2: SP, due to the flaps being left at the takeoff setting during the initial climb, did not restore the clean configuration that supports the 2:1 glide ratio at 125 KIAS. The extra drag showed as about 250 feet of altitude shortfall at the key point and a speed error of some 12 knots, between the tighter band and the outer limits. SP noticed the flap position on the configuration check and cleaned the aircraft in time to regain the profile.
texts.3: SP raised the landing gear, flaps and speed brake as soon as the simulated failure was handled, so the aircraft glided clean at 125 KIAS with the expected 2:1 ratio. Key point altitude was held within 150 feet and the glide speed within +10 / -5 knots, and the range calculation matched the distance actually flown. No drag device was carried into the glide.
texts.4: SP cleaned the aircraft within seconds of the simulated failure and confirmed gear, flaps and speed brake up before starting the glide plan. The clean 125 KIAS glide produced the planned 2:1 ratio, and the aircraft arrived at the key points with altitude and airspeed essentially on target. Configuration was then held unchanged until the planned point for lowering the gear.
texts.marginal: SP cleaned the aircraft and kept the key point values inside the required tolerances, but the speed brake was retracted only after the first altitude check rather than as part of the clean up step. The glide range lost in that interval showed as a steady drift toward the low side of the acceptable band. SP is expected to remove all excess drag before starting the range assessment so that the glide is planned on a 2:1 aircraft rather than on a draggy one.

error_modes.label: Descent rate check after setting 4 to 6 percent torque

texts.0: SP, due to the descent rate never being checked after 4 to 6 percent torque was set, did not verify the glide against the expected 1350 to 1500 fpm. The aircraft descended well above 1500 fpm with no torque adjustment, arriving more than 300 feet below the key point altitude and more than 10 knots slow, outside the +300 / -200 feet and +15 / -10 knots limits. The IP intervened to reset the power and restore the glide profile.
texts.1: SP, due to the VSI being read only once and then dropped from the crosscheck, did not adjust torque when the descent rate settled above 1500 fpm. The excess sink produced a 200 feet altitude shortfall at the key point with the airspeed 10 knots slow, on the -200 feet and -10 knots limits. Torque was increased toward the 1350 fpm target only after the IP prompted the check verbally.
texts.2: SP, due to torque being set at the low end of the 4 to 6 percent band without confirming the resulting sink rate, did not hold the planned 2:1 glide. The descent rate ran near 1600 fpm long enough to cost about 250 feet at the key point, with the speed some 12 knots off schedule, between the tighter band and the outer limits. SP compared the actual rate with the 1350 to 1500 fpm reference and increased torque in time to regain the profile.
texts.3: SP set 4 to 6 percent torque, checked the descent rate and confirmed it inside the 1350 to 1500 fpm reference for a clean 125 KIAS glide. Key point altitudes were held within 150 feet and the airspeed within +10 / -5 knots, and the glide distance flown matched the 2:1 planning figure. The check was repeated as the configuration changed.
texts.4: SP set the glide power and read the VSI within a few seconds, trimming to keep the descent right on the 1350 to 1500 fpm reference. Altitude at the key points differed from the profile by only a few tens of feet and the airspeed stayed within a few knots of the target. The measured glide performance was used to confirm the plan rather than assumed.
texts.marginal: SP set 4 to 6 percent torque and stayed inside the required tolerances, but the descent rate was checked only at the key points instead of immediately after the power was set. Each check found the sink rate near the upper end of the 1350 to 1500 fpm reference and the altitude near the low side of the acceptable band. SP is expected to verify the descent rate as soon as glide power is set so that the profile is protected before the deviation appears.

error_modes.label: Dissipation of excess energy before high key on a high altitude entry

texts.0: SP, due to no attempt to dissipate the excess energy before high key, did not use a slip, an S turn, early gear or a 360 degree turn over the field to lose the surplus altitude. The aircraft reached high key more than 400 feet high and not aligned with the landing runway, so the profile could not be flown normally from that point, beyond the +300 feet and the +15 knots limits. The IP took the controls to reposition the aircraft for the pattern.
texts.1: SP, due to the energy dissipation being started only overhead the field, did not arrive at high key on altitude and aligned with the landing runway. The aircraft was 300 feet high and 15 knots fast at high key, on the +300 feet and +15 knots limits, and the alignment was corrected inside the turn to low key. The S turn and the early gear extension were used only after the IP called the excess energy.
texts.2: SP, due to a single S turn being judged sufficient for the surplus altitude carried into the descent, did not fully dissipate the excess energy before high key. Arrival was about 250 feet high and some 12 knots fast, between the tighter band and the outer limits, with the runway alignment slightly off. SP added a short slip on the way to low key and had the profile back on parameters before cross key.
texts.3: SP assessed the surplus energy early and dissipated it before high key using a combination of an S turn and early gear extension. High key was reached within 150 feet of 3000 feet AGL, wings level, aligned with the landing runway and within +10 / -5 knots of the glide speed. The pattern was then flown from the normal picture without further energy corrections.
texts.4: SP planned the descent so that the excess energy was removed well before high key, using a 360 degree turn near the intended landing point and accepting the associated altitude loss. High key was crossed on altitude within a few tens of feet, aligned with the runway and on speed, with the aircraft settled and the crosscheck free for the pattern. No disorientation or rushed correction was evident at the entry.
texts.marginal: SP dissipated the surplus energy and arrived at high key inside the required tolerances, but the S turn was completed so close to the key point that the aircraft was still settling as it crossed it. Altitude and airspeed remained near the high side of the acceptable band and the runway alignment was achieved in the last few seconds. SP is expected to complete the energy dissipation earlier so that high key is entered from a stabilized picture rather than during the correction.

error_modes.label: Slip technique and recovery altitude when losing surplus altitude

texts.0: SP, due to bottom rudder being applied after the wing was lowered, did not fly the slip as uncoordinated flight with opposite top rudder and turned it into a skid. Airspeed was not held near 125 KIAS and the descent rate ran well beyond 2000 fpm, so the aircraft was left more than 300 feet below the key point altitude with the speed more than 15 knots off, outside the ELP limits. The IP took the controls to recover the aircraft and stop the manoeuvre.
texts.1: SP, due to the slip being held down toward the runway instead of being stopped with 200 to 300 feet remaining, did not leave enough altitude to slow the rate of descent before the round out. The aircraft crossed the last key point 200 feet low with the speed 10 knots slow, on the -200 feet and -10 knots limits. The wings were rolled level and the rudder released only after the IP called for the recovery.
texts.2: SP, due to the nose attitude not being adjusted as the wing was lowered, did not hold 125 KIAS through the slip and let the airspeed wander. The resulting sink rate cost about 250 feet against the profile with the speed some 12 knots off schedule, between the tighter band and the outer limits. SP corrected the pitch attitude, kept the ground track with bank and rudder, and stopped the slip with adequate altitude remaining.
texts.3: SP entered the slip smoothly with the wing lowered and opposite top rudder, holding 125 KIAS by adjusting the nose attitude and keeping the intended track over the ground. Key point altitude was regained within 150 feet and the airspeed stayed within +10 / -5 knots through the entry and the recovery. The slip was stopped with 200 to 300 feet remaining and the wings rolled level while the rudder pressure was reduced.
texts.4: SP used the slip only as far as the surplus altitude required, with the nose kept below the horizon in the full slip and the airspeed steady at 125 KIAS. Entry and recovery inputs were smooth, the ground track did not wander, and the profile was regained with altitude and airspeed within a few tens of feet and a few knots. The slip was terminated with ample altitude to slow the descent rate and confirm positive control.
texts.marginal: SP flew the slip within the required tolerances, but the rudder and bank were not varied enough to hold the ground track and the recovery was begun at the lower end of the 200 to 300 feet guidance. Airspeed remained inside the band while drifting toward the slow side during the recovery. SP is expected to trade bank against top rudder to hold the track and to stop the slip earlier so that the descent rate is arrested with margin in hand.

error_modes.label: High key entry technique and wing tip distance spacing to low key

texts.0: SP, due to the high key offset being taken without reference to the one quarter wing tip distance picture, did not place the runway just above the canopy rail before starting the turn. Bank was then far in excess of the 20 degrees required for the offset entry, so low key was reached inside the two thirds wing tip distance spacing and more than 300 feet off altitude with the speed more than 15 knots off, outside the ELP limits. The IP took the controls to re-establish the pattern spacing.
texts.1: SP, due to insufficient bank in the turn from high key, did not achieve the two thirds wing tip distance spacing with the fuel cap on the runway at low key. The aircraft rolled out wide and 300 feet high with the speed 15 knots fast, on the +300 feet and +15 knots limits. The spacing was corrected only after the IP called the position against the runway reference.
texts.2: SP, due to the overhead entry being flown with slightly less than the 30 degrees of bank it requires, did not hold the planned track from high key toward low key. Low key was reached about 250 feet off altitude with the speed some 12 knots fast and the spacing marginally wide of two thirds wing tip distance, between the tighter band and the outer limits. SP adjusted bank against the runway picture and had the spacing and energy correct before base key.
texts.3: SP established high key at 3000 feet AGL with the runway placed for the chosen offset or overhead entry and turned toward low key with the appropriate 20 or 30 degrees of bank. Low key was reached at the two thirds wing tip distance picture with the fuel cap on the runway, within 150 feet of 1500 feet AGL and within +10 / -5 knots. Cross key altitude confirmed the profile on the way.
texts.4: SP set the one quarter wing tip distance offset with the runway just above the canopy rail and flew the turn to low key with bank varied smoothly around the no wind value. Low key spacing matched the fuel cap reference and the altitude and airspeed were on the profile within a few tens of feet and a few knots. Wings were levelled only momentarily at low key to check spacing before the turn was continued.
texts.marginal: SP kept the high key entry and the low key spacing inside the required tolerances, but on the narrow runway the tendency to fly close in showed and the wings were held level at low key longer than the spacing check needed. Energy stayed within the band while building toward the high side for the roll out on final. SP is expected to hold the two thirds wing tip distance reference and to keep the turn moving at low key so that the pattern does not compress.

error_modes.label: ORM 3-2-1 gates and the continue or eject decision

texts.0: SP, due to the ORM 3-2-1 gates not being used as decision points, descended below 2000 feet AGL while not on profile for the field of intended landing and not in a position to manoeuvre safely to land. The 300 feet decision point passed with no continue or eject assessment, the gear was never confirmed and reported at 200 feet, and the aircraft was more than 300 feet off the profile with the speed more than 15 knots off, outside the ELP limits. The IP took the controls and terminated the approach.
texts.1: SP, due to the gates being treated as altitude callouts rather than as decisions, did not make the continue or eject assessment at 300 feet AGL and confirmed the gear only after passing 200 feet AGL. The aircraft crossed the last key point 200 feet low and 10 knots slow, on the -200 feet and -10 knots limits, and was still not aligned with the centerline at 100 feet AGL. The calls and the alignment came only after the IP prompted each gate.
texts.2: SP, due to attention being held on the aim point while the gates approached, did not make the 300 feet decision call at the correct altitude although the assessment itself was sound. The profile was about 250 feet low with the speed some 12 knots off schedule, between the tighter band and the outer limits, and the gear was confirmed slightly after 200 feet AGL. SP recognized the lag, made the calls and was aligned with the centerline by 100 feet AGL without input from the IP.
texts.3: SP applied ORM 3-2-1 correctly, staying above 2000 feet AGL until on profile with the runway in sight and in a position to manoeuvre safely to land. The continue decision was stated at 300 feet AGL, the gear was confirmed and reported down at 200 feet AGL, and the aircraft was aligned with the centerline at 100 feet AGL with altitude within 150 feet and airspeed within +10 / -5 knots. The gates were used to drive the decisions rather than to describe them.
texts.4: SP treated each ORM 3-2-1 gate as a decision, assessing profile, runway visibility and manoeuvring position before descending through 2000 feet AGL. The continue call, the gear confirmation and the centerline alignment occurred at their altitudes with the profile deviations limited to a few tens of feet and a few knots. The decision to continue was supported by the energy state actually observed at each gate.
texts.marginal: SP made all the ORM 3-2-1 calls and stayed inside the required tolerances, but each gate was assessed slightly after the altitude rather than as it was approached. The margins were kept while the deviations sat toward the low side of the acceptable band at the moment of decision. SP is expected to anticipate each gate so that the continue or eject assessment is made with the aircraft still able to act on it.

error_modes.label: Torque crosscheck and recognition of excessive propeller drag
error_modes.source: technique:5.38 ADDITIONAL OPTIONS FOR ELP TRAINING

texts.0: SP, due to the power lever being set below 4 percent torque and never crosschecked, flew the pattern with the excessive propeller drag of a zero torque profile. The nose low attitude required to hold the glide speed produced a descent far greater than planned, and the aircraft was more than 400 feet below the key point altitude with the speed more than 15 knots off, outside the +300 / -200 feet and +15 / -10 knots limits. The IP intervened on the power lever and terminated the pattern.
texts.1: SP, due to torque not being crosschecked at the radio calls and configuration checks, did not detect that the setting had drifted below the 4 to 6 percent band. The altitude loss between high key and low key exceeded the expected figure by enough to leave the aircraft 200 feet low with the speed 10 knots slow, on the -200 feet and -10 knots limits. The power setting was corrected only after the IP called for a torque check.
texts.2: SP, due to the power lever being nudged during the configuration change, did not keep 4 to 6 percent torque set through the descent to low key. The extra propeller drag showed as roughly 250 feet of altitude shortfall against the profile with the speed some 12 knots off schedule, between the tighter band and the outer limits. SP caught the low torque on the next crosscheck, reset the band and regained the profile before base key.
texts.3: SP set 4 to 6 percent torque on the profile and confirmed it at every radio call and configuration check, so the pattern was flown without excessive propeller drag. Altitude loss between high key and low key matched the expected value and the key points were held within 150 feet with the airspeed within +10 / -5 knots. The pitch attitude required for the glide speed stayed at the normal picture.
texts.4: SP protected the 4 to 6 percent torque setting throughout the profile and read it back on each crosscheck, so any drift would have been caught immediately. Key point altitudes and the glide speed stayed within a few tens of feet and a few knots, and the descent rate remained consistent with the briefed profile. The absence of an abnormal nose low attitude was itself used as a confirmation that the drag state was correct.
texts.marginal: SP kept torque inside the 4 to 6 percent band and the profile inside the required tolerances, but the setting was verified only when an altitude deviation drew attention to it. The descent rate sat consistently on the high side and the altitude near the low edge of the acceptable band between the key points. SP is expected to crosscheck torque at every radio call and configuration check so that excessive propeller drag is recognized from the gauge rather than from the profile error.
